goal.what: The developers build and change the parts of the product so that together they deliver what the README promises the users.

critical_success_factors.what: The developers know what each part must do, for the users or for the product's development and operation, and why.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the opening state the one idea by which the product delivers what its README promises?
necessary_conditions.why: Each part is a piece of one idea, and a developer who knows the idea builds a part that serves it. The solution strategy of [arc42](https://arc42.org) states the few fundamental decisions that shape the whole system.

items.text: Take the one way that the README's How it works states first, from the product vision's concept, by which the product brings its users to their objectives.
Ask how the system as a whole makes that way work: what it takes in from the roles, and what it turns that into.
Write the answer in two or three sentences that a developer can hold in mind while building any part. Point to the README instead of repeating it.

After writing the rest, read each component's line as a developer who knows only the idea, and check that they can see which piece of the idea it carries out. Change the idea or the component where they can't.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each step of each objective's main use, as the README's walkthrough shows it, have one user story that carries it?
necessary_conditions.why: The stories connect the parts to what the users do, so every part can trace back to a step a user takes. Jeff Patton's user story mapping lays the steps of the main use along a backbone, and hangs a [user story](https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/agile/user-stories) on each.

items.text: Take the backbone from the README's walkthrough, and from the main use of each objective that the walkthrough doesn't run.
For each step, ask how the role meets the product at its edge there, such as a command they type, and write one story for each such way, naming the steps it carries.
Add a story for each convenience the product vision asks for, such as resuming a run that stopped.
Go through each exchange of the README's walkthrough, and the main use of each objective it doesn't run, and name the one story that carries each step. Add a story where none does.

necessary_conditions.about: Principles, User stories, Components, Data model, Sequences
necessary_conditions.what: Does each principle, user story, component, and kind of data trace to what the README promises the users, or to a need of the product's development or operation?
necessary_conditions.why: A part that nothing needs costs effort to build and to keep, and gives no one anything. The method is requirements traceability, as Orlena Gotel and Anthony Finkelstein [analyze it](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICRE.1994.292398), applied from the parts back to their sources.

items.text: For each principle and each story, ask which step, doubt, or need it carries, from three sources. The README carries what the users get from the product vision: the steps of its walkthrough, and the doubts that its How it works answers. Development adds what the developers need to build, test, and change the parts. Operation adds what keeps the product working across runs and updates, such as where its work outlives a run.
For each component and each kind of data, ask which principle or which story's sequence reaches it.
Remove whatever reaches none.

critical_success_factors.what: Parts that different developers build fit together.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each principle give a rule and a reason from which two developers decide a case that no line names the same way?
necessary_conditions.why: Developers of different parts meet the same kind of decision, and decide it apart unless a principle settles it. The principles of The Open Group Architecture Framework (TOGAF) give each a statement, a rationale, and its implications.

items.text: Derive the principles from the README's How it works, which answers each doubt of the users from an idea of the product vision's concept, and from the needs of development and operation.

For each answer and each need, ask what every part must hold alike for it to come true, such as where the work's state lives. A part that held it otherwise would break a key result. Each thing that every part must hold alike is a principle.
Leave out what a single component's line already says, since a principle holds only a rule that spans parts.
For each principle, write the rule in one sentence, naming the parts as Components names them.

Write the reason in one sentence: what goes wrong without the rule, for a role of the product vision, naming the key result it guards, or for the developers or the operators. A developer carries the reason to a case that the rule doesn't name.
Point to the principles of any architecture this one builds on, and write only what this product adds or changes.
Take a case that no rule names, and decide it from each reason as two developers of different parts would. Where they differ, sharpen the reason.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each decision that the stories need belong to exactly one component?
necessary_conditions.why: Two components that make the same decision make it twice, and the two copies drift apart. David Parnas's information hiding gives each module one decision that's hard to make or likely to change, and hides it from the rest.

items.text: Take from the stories the decisions that are hard to make or likely to change, such as where the product keeps the work's state.
Give each such decision to one component.
Where two components need the same decision, give it to one, and have the other ask that one.
List under the figure what each component alone decides.
Label each arrow with what one component does to another and the data it passes, not a word such as `uses`.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each component state its type and its technology?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer who doesn't know what kind of thing a component is, or what it's built with, chooses alone, and the components stop fitting. The [C4 model](https://c4model.com/diagrams/container) gives each box its name, its type, such as a script, a skill, or a folder of JSON files, and its technology.

items.text: For each component, decide the type and the technology from the product's constraints, such as the runtime its users have.
Draw and lay out the figure as [the refactor-doc best practice](../refactor-doc/best-practice.md) says of diagrams.
Draw a store of data as a box like a component's, since its type sets it apart.
Give the figure a legend for every symbol.
Read the figure without the text around it, and add to the legend whatever symbol a reader would still have to ask about.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the data model show how each kind of data relates to the others, without its fields?
necessary_conditions.why: Two developers who build the writer and the reader of the same data must join it to the other data in the same way, while its fields stay free to change. A concept model in a class diagram of the Unified Modeling Language (UML), which most developers read, shows this.

items.text: List each kind of data that the components pass or keep.
For each pair that relates, name the relation, and give how many of each it joins at both ends.
Draw each once, as a class by its name alone.
Where one holds the other's parts, put a filled diamond at the whole, since readers take a hollow one in different ways.
Group the data in a frame for each component or store that keeps them, in the order the stories meet them, with the data that most others join in the middle.
Leave the fields to where the developer builds the data.
Below the figure, say in a few words what a kind of data is only where a reader could take its name for another's.

necessary_conditions.about: User stories, Components, Data model, Sequences
necessary_conditions.what: Does each user story have a sequence that shows, at each step, which component acts, along which arrow, and with which data?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer building a step must know who acts there, on what, and what comes next. A [UML](https://www.omg.org/spec/UML) sequence diagram draws a story's steps in order, from the role's first request to what the story gives them.

items.text: For each story, draw each step as a message from one component to another along an arrow of Components, with the data it passes, named as in the data model.
Draw each branch, each step that sends work back, and each question put to the role, since each path of the story, and its test, rests on them.
Let stories that share their steps share a diagram.

Read each sequence as the developer who builds one of its steps, and check that they can tell, at each step, which component acts, along which arrow of Components, with which data, and what comes next. Where no arrow carries a step, add the arrow, or give the step to another component.

necessary_conditions.what: Do the figures, lists, and sentences agree with one another, and with the architecture that the product builds on, on what each part does?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer who finds two places that say different things about a part must choose which to follow, and two developers choose differently. [ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010](https://www.iso.org/standard/74393.html) keeps the views of an architecture consistent by correspondences, which relate what each view says about the same element.

items.text: For each part, gather what every figure, list, and sentence says it does, and what each rule of the architecture that the product builds on asks of a part of its kind. That architecture, such as a shared best practice for its kind of product, holds rules that each part must keep as well.
Where two disagree, decide by the reasons of the principles and of those rules which is right, and change the other.

critical_success_factors.what: The developers can place, set up, and start every part without asking anyone.

necessary_conditions.what: Does Deployment show where each component runs, where the product keeps each kind of data, and how the product starts?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer setting up the product needs to know where each part runs, what it can reach, and how it starts. A [C4 deployment diagram](https://c4model.com/diagrams/deployment) shows this.

items.text: List each environment the product runs in, such as the user's computer or CI, with its technology.
Place each component and each kind of data in one deployment unit within its environment.
Add each thing outside the product that the components depend on, with what they use of it, and no infrastructure that they don't need.
Write in one sentence how the product starts.
Check that a developer could set the product up from nothing by the figure and that sentence.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each component and each kind of data have one place for its files?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer making a change must find the one place it belongs. Simon Brown's package by component, in Robert C. Martin's *Clean Architecture*, lays out the code by the components that the architecture draws.

items.text: Lay out the folders by component, so that each component and each kind of data has its own place.
Say in one sentence for each top folder whom its files are for, such as the users who install the product or only its developers.
Show each folder and file that holds a component or a kind of data, by its real name, one line each, nested as on disk, without the files inside a component.
Beside each, say what it does or holds, in the words a developer looks for when making a change.
Check that, for any change to a component, a developer can name the one folder it goes in.

critical_success_factors.what: The developers know that the product does what the document says before users try it.

necessary_conditions.what: Does Tests show, for each deployment unit, which test levels cover it, how thoroughly, and why a level is missing?
necessary_conditions.why: A part that no test level covers can break unseen. The [test pyramid](https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html) puts most checks at the narrow, fast levels and few at the wide, slow ones.

items.text: Name each level by what it checks against: unit against a part's contract, architecture against this document, and product vision against the product vision, in real use.
List each deployment unit as a row.

For each level, ask what the unit must do by that level's ground, and fill the cell with the tool and how far it tries the unit, and nothing more. `FULL` tries each case and edge, `HAPPY` the main paths, and `SMOKE` one run that confirms what the lower levels checked.
Give unit and architecture most of the checking, and run them on every change.
Where a cell stays empty, say why.
Leave out a unit whose every cell would be empty, and say why under the table.
Check that each story's sequence runs from start to end at the architecture level in some row.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each test level say what runs real, what test doubles replace, what the tests cover, and when they pass?
necessary_conditions.why: A failing test should name the rule, path, or use that it breaks. Each level runs real only what it checks against and replaces the rest with [test doubles](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestDouble.html), and draws its unit tests by the test techniques that the [glossary](https://glossary.istqb.org) of the International Software Testing Qualifications Board (ISTQB) defines: equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, and decision table testing.

items.text: Draw each test from the one thing its level checks against: the ways a part's contract divides at unit, the paths the sequences draw at architecture, and an objective's main use at real size at product vision.
Run only that thing real, and replace the rest with test doubles.
Point to the test rules of the best practices that the product follows, and write only where this product differs from them.

At unit, divide each input and each result that the contract names into classes that the part treats alike, the refused ones among them, and write one test for each class. This is equivalence partitioning.
Where a class ends on an ordered scale, such as a length or a count, write one test at each end and one at the nearest value of the next class. This is boundary value analysis.
Where the contract's result depends on a combination of conditions, write one test for each combination that can occur, with the result it gives. This is decision table testing.
At unit, pass when the tests all pass and run every line and branch.

Close each gap that coverage, mutation testing, or a property-based test finds from the contract, as the code best practice says of the faults that the tests catch. These tools confirm the tests drawn from the contract, and draw none themselves.

At unit, where no guard holds each rule of a part that an AI does on every run, run the part on the real model, with one input for each class, both where the contract says the part acts and where it says it doesn't, and doubles for the parts it works with.

At architecture, run real what joins the components, such as hooks and scripts, and replace each component that an AI runs and each thing outside the product with a double, so that the level calls no model and gives the same result on each run.

At architecture, write one test for each path through each story's sequence: the main flow, each branch, each step that sends work back, and each question put to the role, until every move from one step to the next lies on some path.

Run each check at the time that what it checks calls for, not by how long it takes. Before each push, run the static analysis, the unit and architecture tests that the change reaches, and their coverage, since these show whether the change does what its design says, and the work waits on them. Running every test there meets this too, as a selection by what the change reaches misses a test that reads a file the change edits. On each push, in CI, run every test, and mutation testing and property-based tests over the lines that the push changed, apart from the work, since these check the tests and not the change, and tests drawn from the design before the code leave few gaps for them to find. Each night, in CI, run every check that runs on its own over the whole, property-based tests at their most inputs among them, since a run over a push's lines misses a test changed alone and a fault between parts that no one push changed together.

At product vision, once unit and architecture pass, run the real product on each objective's main use, as the README's walkthrough shows it, at the size of a real request, with an AI in the role that holds an intent the product never receives.

At product vision, measure each key result as the product vision words it, and compare each measure with the last one by the direction the product vision gives, since the product vision sets no target.
At product vision, run each role on the model its users run, since another model makes other mistakes than the users meet.
At product vision, judge each run from its records.
At product vision, try no case that a lower level can test, since each run is slow and costly.
For a test whose result varies from run to run, write how many runs out of how many must meet the expectation.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each thing that the document says the product does rest on a part that a unit or architecture test can check?
necessary_conditions.why: The product vision tests are slow and few, so they can only confirm what the lower levels already showed, and a thing that only a prompt holds, such as a rule an AI keeps by its instructions, varies from run to run where no unit or architecture test can show it. The [Humble Object](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/HumbleObject.html) pattern of Gerard Meszaros's *xUnit Test Patterns* moves the logic out of a part that's hard to test into a part that a test can run.

items.text: For each thing the document says the product does, name the part that holds it.
Where only a prompt holds it, give it to a part that a test can run, such as a guard of the architecture the product builds on, and draw that part in Components.
Leave a judgment that only an AI can make, such as whether a point is the user's, with the AI.
Decide where to test such a judgment: on the real model, as N13.9 says, or, where the architecture the product builds on runs no prompt alone, only in the product vision tests.
Where only the product vision tests show such a judgment, say so in Tests.
The lower levels show a part only if each double behaves like the part it replaces, so give each double only results in the form the part's contract gives, refusals among them.
Test each double as the part's unit tests test the part.

Draw a double of something outside the product from its documentation or from a recorded run of the real thing. A double that gives what the real thing never would passes a test that the real one fails.
For a fault that a higher level finds, name the case or path that the lower level missed, add its test at the level that must catch it, see it fail, and then fix it there.

Trust a check, such as a test, a hook, or the judge of a trial, only once you have seen it fail on a case that breaks what it checks. Trust a judge once it's right on kept records whose answer you know.

critical_success_factors.what: The developers can change the product without making the document wrong.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each choice whose other way would cost a key result say what the other way would lose?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer who doubts a choice and can't see what it was for may undo it and bring back the problem it solved. An [architecture decision record](https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions), by Michael Nygard, keeps a decision with its context and consequences.

items.text: For each choice whose other way would bring back a problem that costs a key result, such as a technology, a tool, or how far a level tests a unit, name the other way it beat, what the choice gives, ending with the key result it serves, and what it costs.
Write it beside the choice, one sentence for each.
For each choice that a figure shows, ask what the other way would bring back. Give a reason and a cost only where it would cost a key result.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the document hold only what stays true while the product vision and the principles stay, and leave each component's internals out?
necessary_conditions.why: A line about how a component works inside becomes untrue at the next change to that component, and the developer then can't trust the document. David Parnas's [information hiding](https://doi.org/10.1145/361598.361623) keeps such details inside the module.

items.text: For each line, ask whether it would become untrue if a component's internals changed while the product vision and the principles stayed.
If it would, move it to where the developer builds the component.

Imagine a change to how a component works inside, such as its steps, a value it uses, or a data's fields, and mark each line it would make untrue. Repeat with a change of another kind until you mark no line.
